entry.title: GRIPS Summer Research Program with Cecilia and Ellen

link.title: GRIPS Summer Research Program with Cecilia and Ellen

entry.content:
This summer, our group had the pleasure of hosting two talented international students through the Global Research Immersion Program for Young Scientists (GRIPS). Over the past few weeks, Cecilia Vaz and Ellen Chan carried out independent research projects with great dedication and curiosity. Cecilia dove into the fascinating world of insect-pathogenic fungi interactions, and Ellen took on the challenge of investigating microclimate refugia for ants, examining how fine-scale environmental conditions might buffer ant communities from climate extremes.

We are very thankful for them bringing incredible energy, passion, and fresh perspectives to our group. We wish them all the best in their future academic and career journeys. Looking forward to welcoming more bright young minds through GRIPS in the years to come!

entry.title: Jinlin Appointed as Associate Editor for JAE

link.title: Jinlin Appointed as Associate Editor for JAE

entry.content:
I’m delighted to share the news that I have been appointed as an Associate Editor for the Journal of Animal Ecology (JAE) —- one of the flagship journals of the British Ecological Society.

JAE holds a very special place in my academic journey. It was the journal that published my very first lead-author paper on species coexistence. That experience gave me a first-hand appreciation for the journal’s high standards and the constructive, rigorous feedback that sharpens a paper into its best possible version. I still remember attending my first BES Annual Meeting in 2019, completely awed by the breadth of exciting research, and the thrill of presenting my own first DPhil results at the virtual meeting in 2020. The warmth and support I received from the community, and the high standards left a lasting impression on me.

So becoming an Associate Editor feels like a meaningful way to give back to the journal and society that shaped me. I’m truly honoured to take on this role, and I look forward to contributing to the community that has given me so much.

On a related note, I’ve also observed that a growing number of young Chinese researchers have joined JAE’s editorial board this time. Since moving back to China, it is really exciting for me to see the rapid development and keen interest in Animal Ecology taking place in China right now. It’s an exciting time to be part of this field, and I feel fortunate to witness, and contribute to, this momentum.
entry.summary: I’m delighted to share the news that I have been appointed as an Associate Editor for the Journal of Animal Ecology (JAE) —- one of the flagship journals of the British Ecological Society.

entry.title: Student retreat and student conference @ BASHANG

link.title: Student retreat and student conference @ BASHANG

entry.content:
Last week, our research group headed to the beautiful Bashang Grassland for a joint student conference with Dr. Wenyuan Zhang’s ZIEL group. It was a wonderful opportunity to step away from the lab, immerse ourselves in nature, and share the science we’ve been working on.

Each member of our group presented their ongoing research, and I couldn’t be prouder of the fantastic work they’ve been doing:

Jie Hui walked us through a review on the effects of fluctuating temperatures on insect overwintering—a timely topic as we think about climate variability.

ZeRu Gong tackled the fascinating relationship between phenotypic plasticity and evolutionary change, sparking some great discussions.

WeiMing Lin introduced the idea of failed trophic interactions as an overlooked ecological force—thought-provoking stuff!

Chen Tian shared his findings on thermal sensitivity in single- versus mixed-species contexts (yes, the one with 20,000+ flies!).

JiaYi Liu presented results from an insect biodiversity survey on XinJiZhou Island, offering a local perspective on community composition and human disturbance.

I also present a new collaborative project that I am myself learning as I am doing! It’s about the joint biodiversity and economic pressure on marine bivalves.

We also learned a great deal from Wenyuan’s group, whose presentations on macro-ecological patterns and methodological cautions in biodiversity studies were insightful. It’s always a pleasure to exchange ideas with fellow ecologists who share a passion for understanding the natural world.

Of course, it wasn’t all work! We made sure to spend time on the stunning grassland: enjoying the fresh air, breathtaking views, and even horse riding. The retreat was a perfect blend of science, collaboration, and fun, and I returned feeling inspired and grateful for such a wonderful team.

Looking forward to the next one already! (tentively TianMu Mountain at ZheJiang)

entry.title: Outstanding Undergraduate Thesis Award Goes to Chen Tian

link.title: Outstanding Undergraduate Thesis Award Goes to Chen Tian

entry.content:
We are pleased to announce that our to-be Master student Chen Tian has received “Outstanding Undergraduate Thesis Award” from LanZhou University for his impressive work on fruit fly temperature sensitivity conducted at our lab.

Chen took full ownership of the project from the very beginning. He established the entire experimental setup, including crossing mass‑bred lines from fly cultures collected in the field just a few months prior. His dedication continued through the data collection phase, where he carefully counted over 20,000 flies to examine how temperature affects behavior in both single‑species and mixed‑species environments.

His findings has offer valuable new insights into thermal responses in inter-connected biological communities, and we are excited to see where his research journey takes him next. Congratulations to Chen on this well‑deserved recognition and happy Graduation!
entry.summary: We are pleased to announce that our to-be Master student Chen Tian has received “Outstanding Undergraduate Thesis Award” from LanZhou University for his impressive work on fruit fly temperature sensitivity conducted at our lab.

entry.content:
Jinlin just attended the Nanjing University-University of Birmingham Research workshop! Working with Dr. Shan Huang and Dr. Yuru Guan, we will dive into marine mollusks—super important for biodiversity and also for seafood/fisheries. entry.title: Lab fieldwork at XinJiZhou
entry.content: This was our group’s first attempt at an insect biodiversity survey. The rain had just lifted, and the island was lush with spring vitality. We had an unexpected companion: a local dog that followed us through the fields for the whole day! But the ground was a muddy mess, and to make matters worse, our supervisor managed to run the three-wheel car into a roadside ditch. Memorable, to say the least.
